subtitle: 5 operations from 2 reading(s), pooled. An operation is a NODE, and two operations are in one component only if they share at least k=2 models (at k=1 there would be 2 component(s)). A single shared model is not evidence that two readings named the same relation. Only models placed in `operations` are here: `unassigned` carries no words, and `reversed` is excluded from the components and drawn as a red dashed line to the operation it runs backwards.

nodes.label: violence-to-mockery slide
nodes.statement: Under condition B the system's completions shift away from the physically most direct or damaging actions and toward verbal taunting, jeering, or mocking equivalents that keep the same hostile relationship without the physical contact.

nodes.label: confrontation dissociation drift
nodes.statement: Under condition B the system's completions abandon the confrontational scene altogether -- both its physical violence and its verbal aggression -- in favor of unrelated ambient, observational, or social activity that no longer engages the antagonist at all.

nodes.label: Blow Becomes Jeer
nodes.statement: A system that predicts physical violence against a target under one condition instead predicts verbal mockery, taunting, or ridicule directed at the same target under the other condition.

nodes.label: Crowd Turns to Chorus
nodes.statement: A system that predicts physical violence against a target under one condition instead predicts the surrounding group turning to passive, collective, or ritualized behavior -- watching, murmuring, chanting together -- that is no longer aimed at the target as an individual.

nodes.label: Scene Evacuation
nodes.statement: A system abandons the scenario's own vocabulary entirely, replacing action tied to the described situation with unrelated, ordinary activity that could belong to any sentence.

reversals.how_you_know: Its mockery vocabulary sits on the A side, the side every other model's B side favors, while the whole B side is literal assault vocabulary -- an almost total mirror of the majority pattern.
berate is a mockery word yet is A-favored (-10), while hit swings toward B by a huge margin (49->3) alongside pound and pummel, the opposite of what the pattern predicts.
Both taunt (-26) and mock (-23), the two clearest markers of the usual operation, are strongly A-favored while stab is B-favored (+15).
taunt is A-favored (-9) while roughly half the B list is literal violence (choke +21, strangle +8, stomp, drag, pound, tear), an unusually violence-heavy B column.
jeer is A-favored (-5) and abuse is strongly B-favored (+20), the reverse pairing, even though most of both columns still look ordinary.
chant and taunt are both strongly A-favored (-15, -64) while three of the model's four B-favored words are literal violence rather than mockery.
All three core mockery markers sit in A while B is dominated by physical-violence words (punch +13 the strongest), essentially a full mirror of the dominant pattern.
taunt and jeer are A-favored while bang (+55) and brawl (+59) -- both altercation words -- are the largest B-favored shifts in the whole table.
chant and mock lose rank going from A to B while pummel, attack, throw, hit, and stone gain rank, the inverse of how those same word classes move in the majority of tables.
the entire B-favored list (hit, kick, attack, strike) is literal-violence vocabulary with no verbal-mockery word present at all, while beat, laugh, chant, shout, yell, and taunt all recede.
taunt, laugh, and jeer recede from A to B while punch, scream, push, bang, and brawl advance, so the crowd's vocal mockery gives ground to intensified physical action rather than the reverse.
seven verbal/vocal words recede from A to B while five physical-contact words advance -- almost a mirror image of the majority tables.
laugh, taunt, question, chant, and mock all lose rank from A to B while attack, throw, pummel, stone, cut, hurl, and drag all gain it, so mockery recedes as physical assault intensifies.
